prompt.context_jp: 富士山の裾野にひろがる富士浅田の街に、いつもと変わらない朝___来た。
prompt.prompt_jp: 富士浅田の街に、いつもと変わらない朝___来た。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits this scene-setting opening.

feedback.correct_en: The sentence introduces the morning as a new piece of information presented to the reader — classic 'neutral description' が for a scene-setting opener.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would mark 'morning' as an already-established topic, but the chapter is just opening and nothing has been introduced yet, so it feels off here.

contrast_examples.en: It started to rain. (new event, newly perceived)
The rain has already stopped. (rain is the known topic)

prompt.context_jp: テレビでは地元の冬祭りについて連絡があり、屋台の数や特産品が次々と紹介されていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 街の話題___こういった催しか選挙か、どちらかしかないような時期だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks 'the town's topics' as the theme of the sentence?

feedback.correct_en: The narrator makes a general statement about the town's topics as the ongoing theme — a classic topic-marking は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present it as newly-introduced information, but 'street talk at this time of year' is the frame being discussed, not fresh news.

contrast_examples.en: This shop is cheap. (general statement about a known topic)
Oh, there's a cheap shop! (new discovery)

prompt.context_jp: 冬の朝の支度は毎回、少しずつ遅れがちだった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 若葉___制服姿でリビングに顔を出した。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle used when a character enters the scene.

feedback.correct_en: Wakaba appearing in the living room is a fresh event the narrator reports — new-information が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat Wakaba as the known topic being commented on, but here the point is her arrival itself, not something about her.

contrast_examples.en: The door opened. (event report)
The door, I already closed. (comment on topic)

prompt.context_jp: 若葉が制服姿でリビングに顔を出した。
prompt.prompt_jp: 母娘の会話___朝はいつも短く、部活や忘れ物の確認だけで終わってしまう。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle frames 'the mother–daughter conversation' as the topic of this generalization?

feedback.correct_en: The narrator makes a habitual, general statement about these conversations — topic は is required.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would read as reporting a specific new instance, but the sentence is a general truth ('always short').

contrast_examples.en: His stories are always long. (generalization)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の話が長くなってきた。
contrast_examples.en: His story has started getting long. (specific moment)

prompt.context_jp: 高橋の姿がバックヤードに消えると、
prompt.prompt_jp: フロント___は朝番の由美と二人きりになった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the location where she ended up alone with Yumi?

feedback.correct_en: With 二人きりになる (existence/state of being alone together), the location is marked with に — the place where the state holds.
feedback.incorrect_en: で marks where an action takes place; here the focus is the resulting state of being there, so に is natural.

contrast_examples.jp: 部屋に二人きりでいた。
contrast_examples.en: The two were alone in the room. (state/location of being)
I studied in the room. (location of action)

prompt.context_jp: チェックアウトの波が一段落し、
prompt.prompt_jp: ロビーには束の間の静けさ___戻った。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits a scene-setting 'X returned' report.

feedback.correct_en: The quietness returning is a new event being presented — neutral-description が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would require 静けさ to already be an established topic, but here it is being newly introduced.

contrast_examples.en: Quiet returned. (event)

contrast_examples.jp: 静けさはもう戻らない。
contrast_examples.en: The quiet won't come back. (contrastive comment)

prompt.context_jp: ロビーには束の間の静けさが戻った。
prompt.prompt_jp: この時間帯___会話を始めても客の出入りで途切れがちで、まとまった話をするには向いていない。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle sets 'this time of day' as the topic of a generalization?

feedback.correct_en: The narrator comments generally about what this time-slot is like — topic は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would single it out as the newly-identified time, but the sentence is characterizing the slot, not identifying it.

contrast_examples.jp: この時間帯は混みます。
contrast_examples.en: This time slot gets crowded. (general property)

contrast_examples.jp: この時間帯が一番混みます。
contrast_examples.en: This slot is the most crowded one. (exhaustive identification)

prompt.context_jp: 幽霊の話がひと区切りついても、
prompt.prompt_jp: 由美の関心___そこで止まらなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits for 'Yumi's interest didn't stop there'?

feedback.correct_en: Yumi has just been talking; 'her interest' is already in play as the topic/theme — は carries the discourse forward.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would introduce the interest as new, but the whole paragraph is already about Yumi talking.

contrast_examples.jp: 話はそこで終わらなかった。
contrast_examples.en: The conversation didn't end there. (continuing topic)
The conversation suddenly ended. (new event)

prompt.context_jp: 午後になると、
prompt.prompt_jp: 次のチェックインの客___少しずつ現れ始めた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits for guests beginning to appear?

feedback.correct_en: New guests appearing is a fresh event being reported — が for neutral description.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat 'the next check-in guests' as an established topic, but they're being introduced into the scene here.

contrast_examples.en: A customer came. (event report)

contrast_examples.jp: お客さんはもう帰った。
contrast_examples.en: The customer already left. (comment on known topic)

prompt.context_jp: 素性は分からない。
prompt.prompt_jp: ただ お金持ちな___確か
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits for 'but at least this one thing is certain'?

feedback.correct_en: Contrast with the previous '素性は分からない': 'his background we don't know, BUT that he's rich is certain' — classic contrastive は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make it an exhaustive 'it IS his being rich that is certain,' but the discourse point is contrast with the unknown background.

contrast_examples.jp: 名前は知らないが、顔は覚えている。
contrast_examples.en: I don't know his name, but his face I remember. (contrast)
He's a person whose face is easy to remember. (identifying property)

prompt.context_jp: 仕事を終えた清美は、
prompt.prompt_jp: 駅前の居酒屋に幼なじみの美波と、後輩の葉月___誘い出した。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the people she invited out?

feedback.correct_en: 誘い出す takes a direct object (the person invited), so を marks Minami and Hazuki.
feedback.incorrect_en: に would mark a recipient or destination, but 誘い出す treats the invitee as the object being drawn out.

contrast_examples.en: I invited my friend. (object)
I called my friend. (recipient)

prompt.context_jp: だが、顔を上げると驚いたことに、
prompt.prompt_jp: 職場の高橋___すぐそばに立っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks Takahashi's surprising presence?

feedback.correct_en: The whole point is the surprising discovery that Takahashi was right there — new-information が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat Takahashi as the already-established topic, but his sudden appearance is precisely what's being revealed.

contrast_examples.jp: 振り向くと、彼が立っていた。
contrast_examples.en: When I turned around, he was standing there. (discovery)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼はいつもそこに立っている。
contrast_examples.en: He always stands there. (comment on known topic)

prompt.context_jp: 倒れた自転車を、
prompt.prompt_jp: 高橋は片手___軽々と持ち上げ、
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks 'with one hand' as the means?

feedback.correct_en: で marks the instrument/means — he lifted the bike using one hand.
feedback.incorrect_en: に would mark a destination or recipient; 片手に持つ exists meaning 'in one hand', but with 軽々と持ち上げ, the means reading で is what's used here.

contrast_examples.en: Write with a pen. (means)
Hold in one's hand. (location)

prompt.context_jp: 高橋は一つ息___吐き、まっすぐに清美を見た。
prompt.prompt_jp: 高橋は一つ息___吐き、
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks 'a breath' as the thing exhaled?

feedback.correct_en: 息を吐く is a fixed transitive expression — the breath is the direct object of 吐く.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make 'breath' the subject, but 吐く here takes an agent (Takahashi) and an object (breath).

contrast_examples.en: He sighed. (object)
A sigh escaped. (intransitive, subject)

prompt.context_jp: 時計の針は九時に差しかかり、
prompt.prompt_jp: ここから昼まで___チェックアウトの客が絶えず現れる、いちばん忙しい時間帯に入っていく。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle sets 'from here until noon' as the topic frame?

feedback.correct_en: The time span is set up as the topic/frame about which the comment is made — topic は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make the time span itself the focus of identification, but the sentence is describing what happens during that span.

contrast_examples.en: In the morning (as for the morning), it's busy.
The morning is the busiest. (exhaustive)

prompt.context_jp: 寒風に頬をこわばらせながら二十分を漕ぎ通して、
prompt.prompt_jp: 清美はようやく勤め先のビジネスホテルに___。
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb best fits 'finally arrived after a hard commute'?

feedback.correct_en: たどり着く conveys arriving after effort/struggle — perfect after battling cold wind for 20 minutes.
feedback.incorrect_en: 立ち寄る means 'stop by (on the way)'; 引き返す means 'turn back' — neither matches her finally reaching her workplace.

contrast_examples.en: I finally reached the summit.

contrast_examples.jp: コンビニに立ち寄った。
contrast_examples.en: I stopped by the convenience store.

prompt.context_jp: フロントで領収書を客に手渡す場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: ___ こちら 領収書になります
prompt.prompt_en: Which set phrase begins the hotel clerk's hand-over to the guest?

feedback.correct_en: お待たせしました is the standard service-industry phrase after any wait, however brief.
feedback.incorrect_en: 失礼しました apologizes for a specific lapse; ごめんなさい is casual and not used in business service register.

contrast_examples.jp: お待たせしました。ご注文のコーヒーです。
contrast_examples.en: Thanks for waiting. Here's your coffee.

contrast_examples.jp: 失礼しました、間違えました。
contrast_examples.en: Sorry — I made a mistake.

prompt.context_jp: フロントでチェックアウト対応中。
prompt.prompt_jp: 確認___ので 少々お待ちください
prompt.prompt_en: Which humble form fits the clerk's own action?

feedback.correct_en: いたします is the humble (謙譲) form the clerk uses for her own action toward the guest.
feedback.incorrect_en: なさいます is honorific (used for the guest's actions, not the clerk's). します is plain and lacks the service-polite register.

contrast_examples.en: I'll show you the way. (humble, speaker)
Will you use it? (honorific, listener)

prompt.context_jp: 丸山がアメニティーを大量に持ち帰る件を支配人に相談したが…
prompt.prompt_en: Which word fits '[hard-to-reprimand] because he's a regular'?
prompt.prompt_jp: やっぱ 常連さんだし 注意___部分があるみたいなんだよねえ

feedback.correct_en: 〜づらい expresses 'hard/awkward to do (psychologically)' — fitting for 'awkward to call out a regular.'
feedback.incorrect_en: しやすい means the opposite (easy to do). しがち means 'tends to do (unintentionally)', which doesn't fit here.

contrast_examples.en: A hard-to-say topic.
Someone who tends to forget.

prompt.context_jp: 久しぶりに三人で飲んで、
prompt.prompt_jp: 清美は久しぶりに、肩の___が抜けていくのを感じた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which word completes 'tension in her shoulders eased'?

feedback.correct_en: 肩の力が抜ける is a fixed idiom meaning 'to relax, let one's guard down.'
feedback.incorrect_en: 肩の重さ/肩の気 are not conventional collocations in Japanese.

contrast_examples.jp: もっと肩の力を抜いて。
contrast_examples.en: Relax a little more.
To lose focus/get a letdown. (different idiom)

prompt.context_jp: 自転車で転んで、
prompt.prompt_jp: ちょっとした段差にハンドルを___、そのまま横倒しに転んでしまった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb form fits 'had her handlebars thrown off by a bump'?

feedback.correct_en: ハンドルを取られる is a fixed expression meaning the handlebars are wrenched/jerked out of your control.
feedback.incorrect_en: 渡される (be handed) and 抜かれる (be pulled out/overtaken) don't match a bicycle losing control on a bump.

contrast_examples.jp: ハンドルを取られて転んだ。
contrast_examples.en: The handlebars got jerked away and I fell.
The baton was handed to me.

prompt.context_jp: 卒業式で前の学年の担任への配慮の話。
prompt.prompt_jp: 私も ああならないように ___なきゃなと思って
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrase means 'have to be careful'?

feedback.correct_en: 気をつける means 'be careful' — Hazuki wants to be careful not to come off like that teacher.
feedback.incorrect_en: 気がつく means 'notice'; 気がすむ means 'be satisfied' — neither fits 'take care not to be like that.'

contrast_examples.en: Take care of one's health.
Notice a mistake.

prompt.context_jp: 高橋がこっそり打ち明ける場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: あの～… 実は俺… ___なのね
prompt.prompt_en: What does Takahashi reveal himself to be?

feedback.correct_en: The chapter's twist: Takahashi reveals he is a 宇宙人 (alien), which explains his impossible strength.
feedback.incorrect_en: 地球人 (Earthling) would be a non-reveal; 外国人 (foreigner) doesn't explain lifting a bike with one hand.

contrast_examples.en: Actually, I'm an alien.
Actually, I'm a foreigner.

prompt.context_jp: 娘が登校するタイミングで、母親が声をかける。
prompt.prompt_jp: 母親の自然な一言はどれ？
prompt.prompt_en: Kiyomi is checking that Wakaba can make it to school on time. Which sounds most natural?

choices.text: 大丈夫でしょうか？　間に合いますか？
問題ありませんか？　時間内に到着可能ですか？

feedback.correct_en: A mother to her teenage daughter at breakfast uses casual, short forms — exactly what the chapter has.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is too polite for mother-to-daughter. C is stiff, written-business Japanese and would sound bizarre at home.

contrast_examples.en: Gonna make it? (family register)

contrast_examples.jp: 時間内に到着可能ですか。
contrast_examples.en: Will you be able to arrive within the time? (business register)

prompt.context_jp: 先輩同僚の高橋に対して、清美が返事をする場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「今日 寒いよね」に対する清美の自然な応答はどれ？
prompt.prompt_en: Takahashi (senior coworker) says 今日 寒いよね. Which reply from Kiyomi sounds most natural at work?

choices.text: ウウッ… 寒いですね
さようでございます、本日は冷え込みますね

feedback.correct_en: To a senior coworker, Kiyomi uses です-form warmly but not stiffly — this is the real line.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is too casual for a senior at work. C is exaggerated keigo better suited to a guest, not a coworker.

contrast_examples.en: It's cold, isn't it. (polite coworker register)
That is correct. (customer-facing keigo)

prompt.context_jp: チェックアウトする客を見送るフロントの決まり文句。
prompt.prompt_jp: ホテルのフロントがチェックアウトのお客様を送り出す定型句はどれ？
prompt.prompt_en: Which is the standard phrase a hotel clerk uses when sending off a departing guest?

choices.text: ありがとうございました いってらっしゃいませ
ありがとう またね

feedback.correct_en: いってらっしゃいませ is the standard hospitality phrase used by hotel staff for guests heading out, paired with ありがとうございました.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is far too casual for a service encounter. C sounds like a farewell to someone leaving forever, not a guest checking out.

contrast_examples.jp: いってらっしゃいませ。
contrast_examples.en: Have a good day / see you again. (hospitality register)
Goodbye. (final farewell)

prompt.context_jp: 由美が同僚の清美に、幽霊を怖がった客の話をする場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 同僚同士の雑談として自然なのはどれ？
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds like real coworker small-talk?

choices.text: 後ろから "いませんか？"って聞いてくるから "いないですねえ"って言って
背後より『存在しますか』との質問を受けたため『存在しません』と回答した
うしろからさー いるのいないの聞いてきてさー いねーっつったわけ

feedback.correct_en: Yumi uses conversational quoting (〜って) and です-light casual-polite — natural for a younger coworker chatting with Kiyomi.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is written/formal and sounds absurd in a lobby chat. C swings too rough/masculine for Yumi's register with a senior female colleague.

contrast_examples.jp: "大丈夫？"って聞かれて "大丈夫"って答えた。
contrast_examples.en: She asked 'you ok?' so I said 'I'm ok.' (natural quoting)

contrast_examples.jp: 安否確認の質問を受け肯定の返答をした。
contrast_examples.en: Received a safety-check inquiry and replied affirmatively. (bureaucratic)

prompt.context_jp: 自転車を片手で持ち上げるのを見られた高橋が、清美に頼む場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 高橋のお願いとして自然なのはどれ？
prompt.prompt_en: Takahashi has just been caught lifting a bicycle one-handed. Which plea sounds most natural in that awkward moment?

choices.text: あの～… これ 誰にも言わないでもらえる？
これを他者に伝達しないでいただけますでしょうか
これ 誰にも言うな

feedback.correct_en: The hedged, friendly 〜でもらえる？ matches Takahashi's gentle character and the awkward, informal roadside moment — this is the actual line.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is overly stiff keigo that would feel suspiciously formal from a coworker in a jam. C is a blunt command that clashes with his mild personality.

contrast_examples.en: Could you keep this a secret? (soft request)
Don't tell anyone. (blunt order)
